## Context
Nothing groups dashboards today (`dashboards` has name, description, layout, isPublic, version, owner; the list has a name-substring search). The Widget Library already has `tags text[]` plus search / chart-type / connector / tag filters (`app/src/app/(dashboard)/widget-library/page.tsx`).

A tenant today is a string column defaulting to `default`, stamped from `TENANT_ID` — one process, one tenant. Real workspaces (membership, roles, switcher) touch every tenant-scoped query and wait for a customer who needs isolation. This issue is the cheap step: aggregate dashboards for one team.

## Change
- Migration: `tags text[] default '{}'` on `dashboards`; route validation; include in export/import.
- Dashboard list: the widget-library filter bar (search + tags), tag chips on cards, tag editing in the dashboard settings dialog.

## Required tests
- Migration applies on a fresh and an existing DB; the tenant-scope ratchet stays green.
- Route unit: tags validated (array of short strings), tenant-scoped.
- jsdom: filter narrows the list; E2E: create a dashboard with tags, filter by one.

items.title: Building Custom Spark SharePoint Connector
Service tokens: a list of JWT configs, and a registry exemption for roles without table access
items.body:
## Why

The Tandem controlplane wants a machine identity for its Slack connector and
agent sidecar: a Rauthy confidential client (`client_credentials`) whose
short-lived JWTs the engine can accept. Today `DONAT_GRAPHQL_JWT_SECRET` is a
single config — cookie `donat_session`, one audience, one literal claims map —
so every verified token becomes the role `user` with `sub` as the tenant, and
a service has to borrow a person's session cookie. That cookie expires, pins
one tenant, and is the wrong shape for a machine.

## Feature 1 — `DONAT_GRAPHQL_JWT_SECRET` accepts a list

Each entry keeps today's shape (jwk_url, issuer, audience, header, claims_map);
the engine tries entries in order and uses the first whose source is present
and whose token verifies (signature, issuer, audience). Which config matched
decides the claims — so a service role is a literal on its config, and nothing
reads roles out of tokens:

```json
[
  {"jwk_url": "http://rauthy:8080/auth/v1/oidc/certs",
   "issuer": "…", "audience": "donat-admin",
   "header": {"type": "Cookie", "name": "donat_session"},
   "claims_map": {
     "x-donat-allowed-roles": ["user"],
     "x-donat-default-role": "user",
     "x-donat-user-id": {"path": "$.sub", "default": ""},
     "x-donat-tenant-id": {"path": "$.sub", "default": ""}
   }},
  {"jwk_url": "http://rauthy:8080/auth/v1/oidc/certs",
   "issuer": "…", "audience": "tandem-agent",
   "header": {"type": "Header", "name": "Authorization"},
   "claims_map": {
     "x-donat-allowed-roles": ["agent"],
     "x-donat-default-role": "agent",
     "x-donat-user-id": {"path": "$.sub", "default": ""},
     "x-donat-tenant-id": {"literal": ""}
   }}
]
```

A single object stays valid and behaves exactly as today. `Header` +
`Authorization` should accept the `Bearer ` prefix.

## Feature 2 — registry exemption for a role with no table permissions

The service token's `sub` is the OAuth client, not a workspace, so the tenant
registry (`workspace.status = active`) would refuse it before any command
runs. A role whose metadata grants no table permissions at all — commands
only — should pass the registry gate with an empty tenant. Tenancy inside its
commands is not weakened: every step still resolves rows explicitly (in
Tandem's case, `connection.account_key = <slack team id>` is the first step of
every agent command), and any lookup that can cross tenants stays under
`unbounded_permissions: declared` with a named reason.

## Acceptance

- Cookie login is byte-for-byte unaffected by adding a second entry.
- A `client_credentials` token with the configured audience, sent as
  `Authorization: Bearer …`, executes commands permitted to the role named by
  its config, and nothing else.
- The same token is refused for any table select/insert (no permissions), and
  a token with a foreign audience matches no config and is refused outright.

items.title: [RFC][FEATURE] Generic OAuth 2.0 client authentication for `http` connectors

type.name: Feature
type.description: A request, idea, or new functionality

items.body:
Tracking issue: #4231 (Support OAuth in connector). Related: #3208, RFC #4915 / PR #4921 (`google_cloud`), #5041, #5079, #5103, #4590.

## Problem statement

Remote-model connectors authenticate in one of three ways today: a static secret substituted into a header (`http`), SigV4 request signing (`aws_sigv4`), or the `google_cloud` strategy added in 3.9, which mints and refreshes a Google access token before each call. Nothing in between exists for the large class of providers whose APIs are protected by a standard OAuth 2.0 authorization server:

- Azure OpenAI / Azure AI Foundry behind Microsoft Entra ID (client credentials, scope `https://cognitiveservices.azure.com/.default`). Organizations can disable key-based access with the Azure policy "Azure AI Services resources should have key access disabled"; requests carrying an `api-key` then return 401 ([docs](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/ai-services/disable-local-auth)), and the existing Azure OpenAI blueprints stop working for those tenants.
- IBM watsonx.ai (IBM Cloud IAM, vendor grant `urn:ibm:params:oauth:grant-type:apikey`), SAP AI Core (XSUAA client credentials), Databricks Model Serving (OAuth M2M), Salesforce Models API (client credentials or JWT bearer): providers whose only API authentication is an OAuth 2.0 token endpoint.
- Self-hosted or gateway-fronted OpenAI-compatible endpoints (vLLM, TGI, Ollama, LiteLLM, Kong/Apigee) protected by a corporate IdP (Entra, Okta, Keycloak, Ping). #3208 describes exactly this: a bearer token that expires, rotated today by stopping the model, updating the credential and redeploying.

RFC #4915 scoped `google_cloud` to Google on purpose and wrote, under "Alternatives Considered": *"Generic pre-request token-provider SPI at the executor base class — over-engineered for a single provider. Rejected in favor of following the established per-protocol pattern; can be generalized later if a second OAuth2 provider appears."* This RFC is that second provider. It proposes the generalization and lets the existing `google_cloud` service-account flow run on it without changing what users write.

## Goals

1. Any `http` connector can declare that its bearer token is obtained from an OAuth 2.0 token endpoint with stored client credentials, and the plugin mints, caches, refreshes and injects the token.
2. Provider differences live in configuration (token URL, grant type, client authentication method, extra parameters, JWT claims), not in code. One implementation covers Entra, IBM IAM, XSUAA, Databricks, Salesforce, Okta, Keycloak and Google service accounts.
3. The token endpoint is treated as a server-side request forgery (SSRF) surface at least as strictly as action URLs are today, because the request body carries a reusable credential.
4. Existing connectors adopt the strategy by update. No new protocol value: the `auth_config` object is stored as its own field of the connector document and of the connector inside model documents, held as a typed field of the connector in memory, and written on the transport as a field that only nodes running the feature's first release or later read and write, the pattern the connector's other recent fields (`tenant_id`, `provisioned_by`) already follow.
5. The generic path adds no third-party dependency.
6. Published `google_cloud` blueprints keep working unchanged; the service-account flow moves onto the generic engine behind the scenes.

## Non-goals

- Forwarding a caller's own `Authorization` header to the remote service (on-behalf-of). That is #4590, a different trust model; this RFC uses none of its field names.
- Environment-derived identity for the generic type (AWS IRSA, #3851). Google Application Default Credentials (ADC) keep working through `protocol: google_cloud` and its library-backed provider; they are not expressible through the generic block.
- Interactive grants (authorization code, device code), the `password` grant (RFC 9700 §2.4: "MUST NOT be used"), the `refresh_token` grant (no model provider surveyed requires it), mutual-TLS client authentication (RFC 8705) and DPoP (RFC 9449). All can be added behind the same configuration surface later.
- MCP connectors. The same hook applies to the MCP executors; it is deferred until the header-forwarding direction in #4590 settles, so the two tracks do not fight over the `Authorization` header. `auth_config` is rejected on MCP protocols in v1.
- Deprecating the `google_cloud` protocol, which stays as a compatibility front door; deprecation is a separate discussion once the generic path has shipped.
- Plaintext or unverified TLS to a self-hosted identity provider. RFC 6749 §3.2 requires TLS on the token endpoint, so `http://` token URLs and `skip_ssl_verification` are refused for OAuth connectors. A private-CA IdP works only with the CA in the node truststore; honouring `credential.ca_cert_pem` without `mutual_tls_enabled` can follow as a generic connector improvement.

## Proposed solution

### What the user writes

A connector declares its authentication in one top-level `auth_config` object whose `type` names the method (`oauth2`; `none` disables) and whose other fields are the method's settings. The object is the API form and the stored form, and in memory a typed field of the connector. Secrets stay in `credential` and are referenced from `auth_config` with `${credential.<key>}`.

Azure OpenAI through Entra ID:

```json
{
  "name": "Azure OpenAI via Entra ID",
  "protocol": "http",
  "auth_config": {
    "type": "oauth2",
    "token_url": "https://login.microsoftonline.com/<tenant_id>/oauth2/v2.0/token",
    "client_auth_method": "client_secret_post",
    "client_id": "<application_id>",
    "client_secret": "${credential.client_secret}",
    "scope": "https://cognitiveservices.azure.com/.default"
  },
  "parameters": {
    "endpoint": "<resource>.openai.azure.com",
    "deployment": "gpt-4o",
    "api_version": "2024-10-21"
  },
  "credential": {
    "client_secret": "<client_secret>"
  },
  "actions": [{
    "action_type": "predict",
    "method": "POST",
    "url": "https://${parameters.endpoint}/openai/deployments/${parameters.deployment}/chat/completions?api-version=${parameters.api_version}",
    "headers": { "Content-Type": "application/json" },
    "request_body": "{ \"messages\": ${parameters.messages} }"
  }]
}
```

No `Authorization` header is written by the user; the executor injects `Authorization: Bearer <token>` at request time.

Google Vertex AI with a service account on the generic path (PR 2b; the published `protocol: google_cloud` form keeps working and is equivalent, see "Relationship to `google_cloud`"):

```json
"protocol": "http",
"auth_config": {
  "type": "oauth2",
  "token_url": "https://oauth2.googleapis.com/token",
  "grant_type": "urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:jwt-bearer",
  "client_auth_method": "none",
  "jwt": {
    "issuer": "<sa>@<project>.iam.gserviceaccount.com",
    "signing_alg": "RS256",
    "lifetime_seconds": 3600,
    "additional_claims": { "scope": "https://www.googleapis.com/auth/cloud-platform" },
    "private_key": "${credential.private_key}"
  }
},
"parameters": {
  "project_id": "<project>", "location": "us-central1", "model": "gemini-2.5-flash"
},
"credential": { "private_key": "-----BEGIN PRIVATE KEY-----\n..." }
```

### Coverage by grant type and client authentication method

What differs between providers is the combination of **grant type** and **client authentication method**; five combinations cover every model provider and identity provider surveyed. Each block below is the `auth_config` object; `credential` holds the values the `${credential.<key>}` references point to.

| Combination | Providers | Lands in |
|---|---|---|
| `client_credentials` + `client_secret_post` | Microsoft Entra ID (Azure OpenAI, Azure AI Foundry: GPT, Llama, Mistral, DeepSeek, Phi); Salesforce client-credentials flow; Auth0; SAP also accepts it | PR 2 |
| `client_credentials` + `client_secret_basic` | Okta, Keycloak, Ping Identity (gateways in front of vLLM, TGI, Ollama, LiteLLM, Kong, Apigee); Databricks Model Serving (service principal, M2M); SAP BTP XSUAA (SAP AI Core); any RFC 6749 server — Basic is mandatory-to-implement for servers (§2.3.1) | PR 2 |
| vendor grant + `none` + API key in the form body | IBM Cloud IAM (watsonx.ai) | PR 3 (`${credential.*}` references inside `token_request_params`) |
| `jwt-bearer` + RS256 | Google Cloud service accounts (Vertex AI, Gemini on Vertex, embeddings), through both front doors; Salesforce JWT bearer flow | PR 2b |
| `client_credentials` + `private_key_jwt` | Entra certificate credentials, Okta, Keycloak, Ping — the keyless path enterprises are moving to | PR 3 |

Not covered, by design: environment identity (Google ADC stays on `protocol: google_cloud`; AWS IRSA out of scope), interactive or device flows, `refresh_token`, OCI request signing (not OAuth), and providers that authenticate with plain API keys (OpenAI, Anthropic, Cohere, Mistral) or SigV4 (Bedrock), which keep today's connectors.

**Microsoft Entra ID → Azure OpenAI / Azure AI Foundry.** The first example above. The v2 endpoint takes `scope: https://cognitiveservices.azure.com/.default`; the default allowlist admits it with the tenant as a GUID in either case or as a domain name such as `contoso.onmicrosoft.com`. The v1 endpoint (`https://login.microsoftonline.com/<tenant>/oauth2/token`) is appended to the allowlist by the operator; it takes `token_request_params: { "resource": "https://cognitiveservices.azure.com/" }` and returns `expires_in` as a numeric string and `expires_on` as an epoch, both handled.

**Okta / Keycloak / Ping-fronted OpenAI-compatible gateway.**
```json
"auth_config": {
  "type": "oauth2",
  "token_url": "https://<org>.okta.com/oauth2/<authorization-server-id>/v1/token",
  "client_auth_method": "client_secret_basic",
  "client_id": "<client id>",
  "client_secret": "${credential.client_secret}",
  "scope": "inference.invoke"
}
```
Keycloak: `https://<host>/realms/<realm>/protocol/openid-connect/token`. Ping Identity: `https://<host>/as/token.oauth2`.

**Auth0-fronted gateway.** `token_url: https://<tenant>.auth0.com/oauth/token`, `client_auth_method: client_secret_post`, and `audience: https://<api-identifier>`, which Auth0 requires.

**Databricks Model Serving (OAuth M2M).** `token_url: https://<workspace-host>/oidc/v1/token`, or the account-level `https://accounts.cloud.databricks.com/oidc/accounts/<account-id>/v1/token`; `client_auth_method: client_secret_basic`, the service principal's application id as `client_id`, `scope: all-apis`. Tokens are valid for one hour.

**SAP AI Core (SAP BTP XSUAA).** `token_url: https://<subaccount>.authentication.<region>.hana.ondemand.com/oauth/token` with `client_secret_basic`. SAP service keys treat the client id as part of the secret, so `client_id` can be a `${credential.client_id}` reference too; any `auth_config` field may be one.

**IBM watsonx.ai (IBM Cloud IAM)**, PR 3, because the API key is passed by reference as an extra form parameter:
```json
"auth_config": {
  "type": "oauth2",
  "token_url": "https://iam.cloud.ibm.com/identity/token",
  "grant_type": "urn:ibm:params:oauth:grant-type:apikey",
  "client_auth_method": "none",
  "token_request_params": { "apikey": "${credential.ibm_api_key}" }
}
```
IBM returns both `expires_in` and an absolute `expiration`; the relative field is used.

**Salesforce Models API.** Client-credentials flow: `token_url: https://<mydomain>.my.salesforce.com/services/oauth2/token`, `client_secret_post`, the connected app consumer key as `client_id`, and `token_response.default_ttl_seconds: 1800`, because Salesforce returns no `expires_in` (the 401 retry covers earlier revocation). JWT bearer flow, PR 2b engine and PR 3 blueprint:
```json
"auth_config": {
  "type": "oauth2",
  "token_url": "https://login.salesforce.com/services/oauth2/token",
  "grant_type": "urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:jwt-bearer",
  "client_auth_method": "none",
  "jwt": {
    "issuer": "<connected app consumer key>",
    "subject": "<integration user username>",
    "audience": "https://login.salesforce.com",
    "signing_alg": "RS256",
    "lifetime_seconds": 180,
    "private_key": "${credential.private_key}"
  }
}
```
Salesforce validates `exp` within three minutes of issue, hence the short lifetime; `subject` is required here, one reason it is configurable and never defaulted.

**Google Vertex AI (service account).** The second example above (`jwt-bearer`, `scope` as an additional claim, `lifetime_seconds: 3600`, no `subject`); `protocol: google_cloud` connectors produce the same request.

**Entra certificate credentials (`private_key_jwt`)**, PR 3: `client_auth_method: private_key_jwt` with a `jwt` block whose `issuer` and `subject` are the application id, `RS256`, `lifetime_seconds: 60`, and `header: { "x5t": "<base64url SHA-1 thumbprint>" }`. Entra identifies the certificate by `x5t`, Okta and Keycloak by `kid`, so PR 3 adds an optional `jwt.header` map restricted to `kid` and `x5t`. For `private_key_jwt` the assertion's `aud` is the token endpoint and `iss` = `sub` = the client id (RFC 7523 §3).

**Response-shape knobs** for providers that deviate from RFC 6749 §5.1: `token_response.access_token_field`, `expires_in_field`, `expires_at_field` (Entra v1 `expires_on`, IBM `expiration`), `default_ttl_seconds` (Salesforce). No provider above needs a non-`Authorization` header or a non-`Bearer` prefix, so custom token headers are not proposed.

### Configuration surface

`auth_config` is written and returned as a JSON object and stored as the top-level `auth_config` object, mapped as `flat_object`, in the connector index and in the connector inside model documents. In memory it is a typed field of the connector, and on the transport a field written and read only between nodes that run the feature's first release or later, as the connector's other recent fields are; a node of an older release reads the connector without it (rule 5, Backward compatibility). `parameters` never carries authentication configuration: a `parameters.auth` value of any shape is an ordinary parameter (rule 10). An update that removes fields from a stored block writes an empty array at each removed field, because some metadata stores merge partial updates object into object; readers treat an empty array as absent. GET never shows the markers; `_search` hits are stored documents and can, so use GET, not a `_search` hit, as the source of an update. Secrets never appear inside `auth_config`: fields that carry secrets hold a `${credential.<key>}` reference, so credential encryption, decryption and GET stripping apply unchanged.

| Location | Field | Required | Default / values |
|---|---|---|---|
| `auth_config` | `type` | yes | `oauth2`; `none` disables and takes no other field; absent → today's behavior. `google_adc` is internal (legacy `google_cloud` ADC) and never user-writable |
| `auth_config` | `token_url` | yes | `https` only, in the canonical form of rule 15; must match `plugins.ml_commons.trusted_oauth2_token_endpoints_regex`. A literal is checked at write time; a `${credential.<key>}` reference is checked for syntax and key existence at write time and in full at mint |
| `auth_config` | `grant_type` | no | `client_credentials`. Any string except a denylist (`password`, `authorization_code`, `urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:device_code`, `refresh_token`); which grants execute is released per PR (rule 13) |
| `auth_config` | `client_auth_method` | yes, whenever the grant authenticates a client | no default; `client_secret_basic`, `client_secret_post` (must be written explicitly); `none` with `jwt-bearer` in PR 2b, otherwise PR 3; `private_key_jwt` in PR 3 |
| `auth_config` | `client_id` | per method | public identifier (RFC 6749 §2.2); visible on GET |
| `auth_config` | `client_secret` | per method | required for `client_secret_*`; must be a `${credential.<key>}` reference |
| `auth_config` | `scope` | no | space-delimited |
| `auth_config` | `audience` | no | sent as the `audience` form parameter |
| `auth_config` | `token_request_params` | no | object merged into the token request body; reserved keys (`grant_type`, `client_id`, `client_secret`, `client_assertion*`, `scope`, `audience`) rejected; literals only until PR 3 adds `${credential.<key>}` references |
| `auth_config.token_response` | `access_token_field` / `expires_in_field` / `expires_at_field` / `default_ttl_seconds` | no | `access_token` / `expires_in` / none / 300 (max 3600). Each field names a top-level member of the token response; `expires_in` may be a number or a numeric string; `expires_at_field` names an absolute epoch; the default TTL applies only when the response carries no expiry at all |
| `auth_config.jwt` (PR 2b) | `private_key`, `issuer`, `subject`, `audience`, `signing_alg`, `lifetime_seconds`, `additional_claims`, `header` (PR 3: `kid` / `x5t`) | JWT modes | `private_key` must be a reference (PKCS#8 PEM); `subject` is emitted only when configured, never defaulted to `issuer` (Google reserves `sub` for domain-wide delegation; Salesforce requires it); `audience` defaults to `token_url`; `RS256` (`PS256`, `ES256` in PR 3); lifetime default 60 s, max 3600; `additional_claims` may not override `iss`, `sub`, `aud`, `exp`, `iat`, `jti` |

The token is always sent as `Authorization: Bearer <token>`.

Rules the implementation enforces without exception:

1. **The configuration is a field of the connector that request parameters cannot reach.** Predict-time input parameters override connector parameters, but `auth_config` is not a parameter: the executor reads the declaration from the connector it was built with, never from the merged request parameters, and the cache key derives from that same declaration, so a caller cannot redirect the credential at predict time. `${parameters.*}` is rejected inside `auth_config` at write time; the only references allowed are `${credential.<key>}`, each naming an existing credential key. The bearer is added to the per-request header map after runtime header substitution, and `Authorization` stays blocked for `${parameters.*}`. The configuration cannot change under a running executor: each executor works on its own cloned connector, and every configuration change arrives as a replacement executor (a standalone connector cannot be updated while models use it; an inline connector changed through model update triggers a redeploy).
2. **A connector with `auth_config.type` other than `none` may not also define an `Authorization` header.** Create and update reject it; the injected header is the only source.
3. **Every action URL of such a connector must be `https`.** URLs that resolve from the connector's own parameters are checked at create/update; the final resolved URL is checked again at execution on every path (predict, stream, execute, batch) before a token is requested, because the shared address validation accepts `http` and a bearer over cleartext is what RFC 6750 §5.2 forbids. Non-OAuth connectors keep their behavior (the same shape as #5083 for mutual TLS). Such a connector may not set `client_config.skip_ssl_verification: true` either: nothing below the plugin guarantees TLS for connector egress, so the plugin must guarantee an authenticated TLS peer whenever it attaches a bearer. The token client never offers skip-verify.
4. **`auth_config` is accepted on `http` and `google_cloud` only.** It is rejected on `aws_sigv4` and the MCP protocols in v1.
5. **Writes that set or change `auth_config` require a fully upgraded cluster.** An older node reads the connector without the block and would run an `http` connector without a bearer (401, fail closed) or a `google_cloud` connector with its legacy identity even after an explicit `none`. Create, update and register therefore check `getMinNodeVersion()` against the first release with the feature and reject with a message naming the upgrade. Every request that carries `auth_config` is checked, an identical re-send included; a request that leaves `auth_config` and the protocol untouched is not. The check runs when a request is written, so it cannot see an older node that joins later (see Backward compatibility).
6. **Update validation sees the stored credential keys and never re-encrypts them.** Reference validation uses the stored key set, replaced by the request's keys when the request supplies a non-empty `credential` (the replacement semantics of connector update). The key set is copied before the write-back object is stripped, so only plaintext submitted in the request is encrypted and stored ciphertext is left untouched. Secret material is parsed at write time only when plaintext is available; otherwise the check moves to mint time with a clear error.
7. **Update semantics are explicit.** An `auth_config` in a request is always the whole configuration and replaces the stored block as a whole; there is no type-only form, so an active block that holds only `type`, such as `{"type": "oauth2"}`, fails the method's required fields (a change to an active type is subject to rule 8). `{"type": "none"}` clears the stored configuration; `none` with any other field is rejected. `type` is required in every `auth_config`, on create, register, update and model update; a block without `type`, a non-string `type` and an empty `auth_config` are rejected. Null members are ignored; to remove a field, send the block without it. GET returns `auth_config` as an object, so GET → PUT round-trips.
8. **Changing where a stored secret goes, or what it is used for, requires the secret again.** An update that changes a protected field must carry `credential` in the same request; otherwise 400 naming the first changed field. Protected: `token_url`, `grant_type`, `client_auth_method`, `client_id`, `scope`, `audience`, `token_request_params`, `jwt.issuer`, `jwt.subject`, `jwt.audience`, `jwt.additional_claims`, the set of credential keys referenced from `auth_config`, and `type` whenever the new value is an active method. Switching to `none` is exempt, since it stops the use of the secret and clears the configuration (re-enabling needs the secret again). Not protected: `token_response.*`, `jwt.lifetime_seconds`, `jwt.signing_alg`, `jwt.header`. Comparison is on canonicalized literals (rule 15 for `token_url`) and on reference strings as written; nothing is resolved at write time, so a secret rotated in place outside the connector does not trigger the rule. Carrying `credential` replaces the stored map, and every key the resulting `auth_config` references must then be present, so an unrelated key does not satisfy the rule. A connector without a stored `auth_config` compares as `{"type": "none"}`. Default token-endpoint patterns pin the path as well as the host, which narrows exposure but does not bind a tenant, hence the rule. Externally managed referenced values stay under their owner's authority, and the resolved destination must still pass the live controls before use (rule 11).
9. **The action URL's origin is fixed by the connector.** The scheme, host and port of each action URL must resolve from the connector's own parameters at create/update/register, and at execution the origin resolved with request parameters must equal it; path, query and body substitution are unaffected. The control applies to every connector with action URLs, not only to OAuth connectors. Per action; batch status and cancel inherit the origin of the `batch_predict` action they are derived from. Unresolved path variables do not prevent extracting the origin. The execution-time comparison also covers connectors the write-time check did not see: those stored before it, and writes that skip it, such as a connector supplied by a transport caller in a model update. If a stored origin cannot be determined, execution fails closed with a message pointing to the connector or model update that stores the host, and never completes the origin from request input. The request is built from the URL that passed these checks. A parameter cycle in an action URL is a 400 that names no parameter, at execution and at create, update and register.
10. **What counts as an authentication declaration.** The only authentication declaration is the top-level `auth_config` object. A `parameters.auth` value of any shape is an ordinary parameter, neither read, rejected nor hidden, like the former `"auth": "Sig_V4"` of the Bedrock Claude 3 blueprint, which PR 1 removes. `auth_config` is strict: malformed content or an unknown `type` is a 400, never "no authentication". A declaration is switched to `none`, never removed, so a protocol change to one that does not take `auth_config` (rule 4) is refused while one is stored.
11. **The kill switch acts on injection; the token allowlist acts on minting and hand-out.** `connector.auth_enabled` is read before every header injection; off → the request fails with an error naming the setting, cached tokens are evicted and refreshes stop. Every mint matches the *effective* `token_url` (after reference resolution) against the allowlist it started with, and every hand-out of a token (each cache hit, and the publication of a new token to every waiting request) re-matches the token's URL against the current allowlist, so a token checked under an older list is never handed out; a change of the allowlist evicts the entries that no longer match. A request that already holds a token proceeds (the kill switch still applies at its injection); a request already on the wire cannot be recalled.
12. **`client_auth_method` is required** whenever the grant authenticates a client; there is no default; `none` must be written.
13. **Release gating.** PR 1 rejects every active `auth_config` as "not supported in this version"; execution support lifts the rejection per protocol (PR 2 `http`, PR 2b `google_cloud`) and per grant: PR 2 lifts it for `client_credentials` with `client_secret_basic` or `client_secret_post`, PR 2b for `jwt-bearer` (which uses `client_auth_method: none`), PR 3 for the other grants and for `none` with `client_credentials`.
14. **Rotation on open source** is a connector update followed by a redeploy (or an inline-connector model update), which yields a new executor and a new token-cache key; the credential comes from the connector itself, so there is nothing to re-read.
15. **Canonical URL form for the token-endpoint allowlist.** The URL is parsed with `java.net.URI`; userinfo, a fragment, a query string or a non-`https` scheme is rejected (400). The string matched against the allowlist is rebuilt from the parsed components (lower-cased scheme and host, the default port 443 removed and any other port kept, then the path as written), never the raw input, so a host always ends at the first `/`. Default patterns write the host from literal domains and explicit label classes such as `[a-z0-9-]+`, never `.*`, `.+` or `[^/]+`; the setting validator rejects a pattern with such a construct in the authority, because `https://evil.example?.okta.com/…` or `https://attacker.example/x.okta.com/…` would otherwise satisfy a loose pattern while `URI.getHost()` returns the attacker's host. `https://oauth2.googleapis.com:443/token` canonicalizes to `https://oauth2.googleapis.com/token`; `:8443` is kept and matches only a pattern that names it.

Custom token-request headers are not offered in v1: header control toward an attacker-chosen URL is one precondition for reaching metadata services, and `token_request_params` (body only) covers every provider surveyed.

### Execution flow

```
predict
 └ RemoteConnectorExecutor.preparePayloadAndInvoke                 (unchanged)
    └ HttpJsonConnectorExecutor.invokeRemoteService / ...Stream     (one new step)
       ├ resolve the action URL once: trusted endpoints, stored origin (rule 9)
       ├ no active auth_config on the executor's connector → existing path
       └ else: require https on the resolved action URL (rule 3)
            provider (built once per executor; oauth2; google_adc from PR 2b):
              reads the connector's auth_config, re-runs the write-time checks
            token cache (key: tenant, auth_config, credential fingerprint)
            ├ fresh and token_url still allowlisted → token
            └ miss / near expiry → token request (one in flight per key)
                 · one credential snapshot; resolve ${credential.*} → effective token_url
                 · canonicalize (rule 15), require https, match the allowlist
                 · resolve DNS, validate every address, connect only to validated addresses
                 · build the grant (client_secret basic/post; jwt-bearer in PR 2b; private_key_jwt in PR 3)
                 · POST, async, no redirects, 10 s timeout, 64 KB cap; parse, compute expiry, store
          check connector.auth_enabled before attaching any header (rule 11)
          headers = runtime headers + Authorization: Bearer <token>   (per-request map)
       └ request built from the checked URL and the header map → remote call
          └ on 401, refresh budget unused, token at least 10 s old: drop it, obtain a new one, retry once
    streaming: the same checks and token step, then the stream opens on the checked URL with the header map;
      a 401 drops the token (same 10 s rule) and ends the stream, no replay
```

For `google_cloud` connectors without an explicit type, PR 2b synthesizes the equivalent configuration from the fields the protocol already stores (see below), so both front doors reach the same engine.

Every check before the token step is local, so a request that will be refused costs no call to the identity provider. Both request builders, the streaming one included, take the checked URL and the per-request header map (the separate rule 9 PR, Delivery plan), so streams need no separate header route. Every stream already connects directly and without redirects (#5206), and #5228, before PR 2, makes it connect only to validated addresses. Batch status and cancel build a fresh executor per poll, so the cache is process-wide rather than per executor; otherwise every poll would mint a token, and IdPs such as Entra rate-limit that. The `gemini/v1beta/generatecontent` streaming interface on `http` is left to PR 2b, its first consumer.

### Token acquisition and caching

Code lives in `ml-algorithms` under `org.opensearch.ml.engine.algorithms.remote.oauth2`; `common` cannot perform HTTP and hosts only configuration, validation and the header helper.

- **No new dependency on the generic path.** `client_credentials` needs form encoding and JSON parsing, both already available. JWT assertions (PR 2b, PR 3) are signed with `java.security.Signature` from a PKCS#8 key; v1 accepts PKCS#8 PEM only and documents the `openssl pkcs8` conversion. This avoids the dependency surprises `google-auth-library` produced in #5079/#5103; the library stays only for the legacy ADC provider.
- **Two layers.** A token-exchange client (form POST, JSON parse, expiry, cache, retry), identical for every provider, and a grant-material layer that decides what goes in the form. The only abstraction is `AuthorizationProvider { void authorizationValue(ActionListener<TokenHandle> listener); boolean invalidate(TokenHandle handle); }`; a small factory maps `auth_config.type` to a provider. The token is written into the current request's header map only. A handle holds its own copy of the token and knows the cache entry it came from: `invalidate(handle)` drops that token only if the entry still holds it and it is at least 10 s old, and returns whether the request may be sent again; a late 401 for a replaced token changes nothing. `client_secret_basic` form-encodes the client id and secret before Base64 (RFC 6749 §2.3.1).
- **Cache key** = SHA-256 of the tenant id, the normalized `auth_config` (every field, excluding per-request values such as `jti` and `iat`) and a fingerprint of the resolved secret material. Content-addressed because inline connectors have no id and because a rotated secret then changes the key. Different scopes for one client are different tokens.
- **Refresh-ahead** at `min(60 s, 10 % of lifetime)` before expiry with 0–10 % jitter; one in-flight fetch per key; on refresh failure the old token is served until its real expiry. Failures are negative-cached per key with exponential backoff capped at 60 s, so a misconfigured connector cannot lock out the customer's OAuth client, and the 10 s minimum token age (401, below) bounds token requests against a service that rejects every token. Where the credential store has its own cache, the next mint after `invalid_client` / `invalid_grant` re-reads the credential with a forced refresh.
- **Mint order.** A mint takes one credential snapshot and resolves every reference first, which yields the effective `token_url`; it then canonicalizes it, requires `https`, matches the allowlist (rule 11), resolves the host and validates every address with the node's current connector address settings (the node's own interface addresses are enumerated on each token request), and sends to that same URL.
- **Expiry.** `expires_at` = the time the token request was sent + `expires_in` − margin. The relative `expires_in` is preferred over absolute fields because it is immune to clock skew; absolute fields come second and `default_ttl_seconds` last; a missing expiry never means forever. The access token is opaque (RFC 6750): a JWT `exp` claim is never parsed. Inside the refresh window the current token is served while a background refresh runs; past hard expiry the request waits for the fetch. Entries are shared by every model, batch poller and execute call with the same configuration and survive redeploys; a change to any token-request input moves to a new entry.
- **401** from the remote service (non-streaming): invalidate, refresh, retry once; 403 is not retried. A 401 drops the token only if it is at least 10 s old; a younger token is kept and the request fails, so a service that rejects every token causes at most one token request per configuration every 10 s. The budget is one refresh per logical action, held in the `ExecutionContext` that the outer 429/5xx retry reuses, so `401 → refresh → 503 → retry → 401` fails on the second 401. Streaming: a 401 invalidates the token and ends the stream with an error, without replay.
- **IdP error mapping.** The `error` field of a token response maps onto a fixed set (RFC 6749 §5.2 codes plus `server_error`, `temporarily_unavailable`, `unknown`); raw `error` and `error_description` text never reaches logs, exceptions or metric labels.
- **Scope.** Per node, in memory, bounded LRU (1000). Tokens never reach the connector index, cluster state or any shared store; evicted tokens are wiped on a best-effort basis, and a sweep every 60 s removes expired ones, idle nodes included. The cached lifetime is `min(expires_in, plugins.ml_commons.connector.oauth2_token_cache_max_seconds)` (dynamic, default 3600), so day-long IdP tokens do not extend residency. Per-node caching costs N requests per token lifetime for N nodes; a shared cache would add a second secret transport.
- **`token_type`** absent is accepted; present and not `bearer` (case-insensitive) → error, so a DPoP token is never sent as Bearer.
- **Token sanitization.** The token must be printable ASCII without whitespace (0x21–0x7E) and at most 8172 characters, so that `Authorization: Bearer <token>` stays within the 8192-byte header limit; a hostile IdP response cannot inject headers into the model request.

### Security controls

| Control | Mechanism | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Opt-in | `plugins.ml_commons.connector.auth_enabled`, default `false`, dynamic, gating every connector whose `auth_config.type` is not `none`; checked at the write sites that check `connector.vertexai_enabled` and read live at mint; 403 names the setting. Legacy `google_cloud` connectors stay under `connector.vertexai_enabled`, which also becomes live at mint for them | Same requirement as the security review of #4921; reversible with one setting |
| Token-endpoint allowlist | `plugins.ml_commons.trusted_oauth2_token_endpoints_regex` (dynamic, validated by `validateRegexSafety`), separate from the inference allowlist so operators need not trust an IdP host for inference. Defaults: Entra `login.microsoftonline.com` v2 (tenant as a GUID or a domain name), Google `oauth2.googleapis.com`, IBM `iam.cloud.ibm.com`, the Databricks account host, Salesforce `login.salesforce.com` / `*.my.salesforce.com`, Okta `*.okta.com` (any authorization server); operators append private IdPs and Databricks workspace hosts. Matching uses the canonical URL of rule 15, and every token hand-out re-matches it (rule 11) | #5041 (host validated, port not); #5079 (defaults missed the provider) |
| SSRF | The token client validates every resolved address with the shared rules (`ConnectorAddressValidator`, #5228: loopback, link-local, unique-local, RFC 1918, IMDS, `connector.restricted_ip_patterns`; private destinations only with `connector.private_ip_enabled` and the private-endpoint allowlist) and connects only to the validated addresses. Regardless of `connector.private_ip_enabled` it also refuses loopback (127.0.0.0/8, ::1), the unspecified addresses, the node's own interface addresses (enumerated on each token request) and `fc00::/7`, including every IPv4 address a mapped or NAT64 form carries, and the configured `http.port` and `transport.port` ranges (9200-9300 and 9300-9400 by default) on every destination, which covers the other nodes; transport profile and publish ports are not covered, and an `http.port` range that includes 443 refuses every token endpoint. No redirects, 10 s timeout, 64 KB response cap | Validate-then-connect with a second resolution leaves a DNS-rebinding window, and this request's body is a credential. No legitimate token endpoint lives on the cluster itself |
| Write-time validation | `ConnectorProtocolValidator` checks that `auth_config` is allowed for the protocol (rule 4) and that the cluster is fully upgraded (rule 5); `AuthConfigValidator` runs at every write site (create, update, register, model update; hidden models included): the block parses, field combinations per method, grant denylist, algorithm allowlist, token_url allowlist, private key parses when plaintext is available, every reference names a key in the credential-key view (rule 6), no `${parameters.*}`, no user `Authorization` header, no parameter cycle in an action URL. The executor re-runs these checks when it builds its token provider. Not in constructors, which also run on read-back: a stored declaration that fails these checks is still read, and it does not block an update that leaves `auth_config` and the protocol unchanged | `token_uri` was validated only at first predict and surfaced as an unwrapped `IllegalArgumentException` (#5079, docs #13164); #5135 shows the accepted placement |
| Runtime isolation | `auth_config` from the stored connector only, out of reach of request parameters; `Authorization`-class headers stay blocked for `${parameters.*}` (rule 1) | Provider behavior is declared per connector, not injectable at call time (review of #4921) |
| Credential bound to its destination | Rule 8 on update; rule 9 at execution for every connector | An editor without the secret could otherwise redirect it to another allowlisted host, and a predict caller could retarget the host through parameter override; multi-tenant allowlist entries do not bind a tenant |
| Kill switch and allowlist act on delivery | Rule 11 | Cached tokens would otherwise keep flowing after the feature is turned off or an endpoint is removed |
| Secret hygiene | One minting chokepoint maps failures to `MLException("Failed to obtain OAuth2 token from <host>: <mapped error code>")`; logs carry status, mapped code, host and latency, never raw `error` / `error_description`, request bodies, `Authorization` values or assertions | #5058 (vendor exception chains leaked to callers) |
| Bearer only over authenticated TLS | Rule 3: `https` action URLs at write time and at execution, no `skip_ssl_verification`; the token client has no skip-verify option | RFC 6750 §5.2; the address validator accepts `http`, the endpoint allowlist is editable and skip-verify is honoured by the HTTP client, so no layer below the plugin guarantees TLS |
| No redirects with a bearer | Streams follow no redirects (#5206); the netty inference client has no redirect handling and treats any status above 300 as an error; the token client follows none | OkHttp follows redirects by default and strips `Authorization` only on cross-host hops |
| Observability | Four node stats in `_plugins/_ml/stats`: `ml_oauth2_token_request_count`, `ml_oauth2_token_failure_count`, `ml_oauth2_token_cache_hit_count`, `ml_oauth2_unauthorized_response_count`; one structured log line per token request with the mapped error code, without token material | Operators see IdP trouble without reading secrets |

### Relationship to `google_cloud` and RFC #4915

Google's service-account flow is a standard RFC 7523 §2.1 JWT-bearer grant: a JWT signed with the service account's key (`iss` = `client_email`, `aud` = the token endpoint, scopes in a `scope` claim, no `sub`, which Google reserves for domain-wide delegation) is exchanged for an hour-long access token. Everything Google-specific is configuration: the token endpoint, the scope claim and the key-file field names. Only ADC is a different mechanism: it reads identity from the environment (key file, gcloud credentials or the metadata server) and is not a token exchange the plugin performs.

This RFC therefore proposes **one engine, two front doors** (PR 2b):

- **The generic front door.** `protocol: http`, `auth_config.type: oauth2`, the `jwt-bearer` grant and a `jwt` block, as in the example above. No Google-specific code.
- **The compatibility front door.** `protocol: google_cloud` keeps its constants, `validate()` and blueprints. `GoogleCloudConnector` synthesizes the equivalent configuration from the fields it stores: service-account mode → `oauth2` with `token_url = credential.token_uri` (default `https://oauth2.googleapis.com/token`), `jwt.issuer = ${credential.client_email}`, no `subject`, `jwt.private_key = ${credential.private_key}`, `jwt.additional_claims.scope = parameters.scopes`, `RS256`, 3600 s; ADC mode → `google_adc`, served by the existing library-backed provider behind `AuthorizationProvider`. An explicit `auth_config` on a `google_cloud` connector takes precedence.
- `GoogleConnectorExecutor` becomes a subclass of `HttpJsonConnectorExecutor` with only its constructor, inheriting the HTTP-client cache, header injection, the 401 retry and the streaming header path; its `authorizationValue` field and header override go in the same PR, and `GoogleCredentialProvider` is reduced to ADC. Legacy `validate()` still requires `private_key` and `client_email` when no explicit type is present.

What legacy users see: service-account connectors created on 3.9 keep working unchanged; the token request goes through the validated client instead of the library's own transport; tokens are cached per node instead of per executor, so batch pollers stop minting on every poll; a 401 from Vertex triggers one refresh and retry; `connector.vertexai_enabled` becomes a live kill switch at mint. ADC connectors are unchanged.

RFC #4915 rejected extending `http` with an optional `auth` block because it "overloads the HTTP executor with branching auth logic". This design adds one hook and one factory, not per-provider branches, while the per-protocol road now has visible costs: three copies of the HTTP executor, of which only one has the HTTP-client cache and mTLS (accepted but ignored by MCP and `aws_sigv4`, #4971, #5003), and `http` connectors that could not adopt OAuth2 without being recreated. An auth strategy on `http` composes with the transport, and `google_cloud` becomes a thin alias of it.

## Alternatives considered

### Keep `google_cloud` entirely separate (the previous revision of this RFC)

Pros: no change to a recently merged feature; smallest first review. Cons: two token engines with different SSRF controls, caches and retry behavior; Google's gaps stay (a token exchange outside the validated client, a per-executor cache, no 401 re-mint, the `io.grpc.Context` dependency chain); the generalization #4915 promised never happens. Decision: run the service-account flow on the generic engine behind the existing front door, and keep ADC on the library, because it is not a token exchange and re-implementing the metadata-server path would need an exception to the token client's refused addresses.

### Carrier of the configuration

- **Flat `oauth2_*` parameters** (an earlier revision): no wire change, but every field needs a prefix, nested values are escaped strings, and the type hides among template variables.
- **A full top-level `auth` object**: self-describing, but a second top-level authentication block next to `credential`, which reviewers found confusing.
- **Chosen: one top-level `auth_config` object on the API, stored as an object, held as a typed field of the connector in memory, and written on the transport as a field that only nodes running the feature's first release or later read and write (revision 3.6).** Revisions 2 to 3.5 carried the object in memory and on the transport as a JSON string under the reserved parameter key `auth`, so that no stream `Version` branch could misalign the stream in a mixed cluster. That objection no longer applies: the branch follows the pattern of the connector's existing gated fields (`tenant_id`, `provisioned_by`, the 3.9 fields), the gate's version constant is fixed to the first release that ships the feature, and the write guard of rule 5 keeps declarations out of a cluster with an older node. The string form, in turn, needed a conversion between the two forms at every read and write and a reserved parameter key; the field needs neither, users read and write a real object, and request parameters cannot reach the configuration (rule 1). Revision 2 exposed a separate top-level `auth_type`; reviewers found the three surfaces hard to read, so revision 3 promotes the whole object and drops `auth_type`.

### Other roads not taken

- **Hook in `ConnectorUtils.buildSdkRequest`**: reaches every HTTP caller but puts I/O and a cache in a static utility, and MCP does not use it.
- **Cluster-wide token cache**: one more secret transport to save N−1 requests per token lifetime.
- **Token fetch at create time (dry run)**: early feedback, but create would perform egress and trip IdP rate limits; possible later as opt-in.
- **Native ADC on the generic path**: needs a metadata-server client exempt from the refused addresses; deferred.

## Backward compatibility

- On the transport, `auth_config` is a field of the connector and of the connector create and update input, written and read only when the stream version is at or after the feature's first release, as the connector's `tenant_id`, `provisioned_by` and 3.9 fields are; a node of an older release reads the connector without it, every other field intact, and a newer node reads an older node's stream as a connector without it. The top-level `auth_config` is stored as a `flat_object` (`ml_connector.json` schema 5→6, `placeholders/connector.json`, `ml_model.json` 14→15), and the index mapping is brought up to date before every write that can carry it. During a rolling upgrade an older node that receives such a connector would run an `http` connector without a bearer (401, fail closed) or a `google_cloud` connector with its legacy identity; writes that carry `auth_config` are rejected until every node runs the release (rule 5), and the gate's version constant equals that release. Enable `connector.auth_enabled` only after the whole cluster runs it.
- Rule 5 is checked when a request is written. OpenSearch lets a node of an older minor release join a cluster unless an index created on the newer release exists, and such a node reads connectors without their `auth_config`. Operational rule: a node of an older release must not join the cluster after `plugins.ml_commons.connector.auth_enabled` has been turned on.
- Updates stay partial on every metadata store: dropped fields are written as empty arrays, the one value every store applies as a replacement; readers treat them as absent and normalize the numeric strings DynamoDB returns. GET shows no marker; `_search` returns stored documents and can.
- ml-commons does not manage the mappings of remote metadata stores: operators add `auth_config` as `flat_object` to the remote connector index, to `connector` in the remote model index, and to the search index behind a DynamoDB store before any declaration is written; `none` needs no flag, so this belongs to the upgrade itself.
- Connectors without a declaration behave as before, except for rule 9 (next item) and except that updating the parameters of a connector stored without parameters no longer fails with a server error.
- Rule 9 applies at execution to every connector with action URLs, with or without `auth_config` or a credential: request parameters can no longer change the scheme, host or port of its action URLs; parameters that fill the path, query or body are unaffected. A connector whose host comes from a request parameter, for example a region supplied at predict time, must store that parameter (connector update, or model update for a connector defined inside the model). A parameter cycle in an action URL returns 400 instead of a server error. The write-time half is already in place (#5183).
- New settings default to off / the public-IdP list / 3600. A customer's own `auth` parameter, whatever its value, is never reinterpreted (rule 10).
- PR 1 and PR 2 ship in the same release, so every stored `auth_config` was written through that release's write checks; the executor re-runs them, under the current token-endpoint allowlist, when it builds its token provider.
- Rotation on open source is a connector update followed by a redeploy, which yields a new token-cache key (rule 14).

## Delivery plan

| Step | Content |
|---|---|
| PR 1 (#5223) | `common` + `plugin`: `auth_config` stored as an object, held as a typed connector field and written on the transport as a version-gated field; a stored reader that drops removal markers and normalizes numeric strings, and strict request parsers, model register included; mapping bumps and the mapping refresh before connector and model update writes; the typed model; the write-time gates of rules 4–8, 10 and 13, with a request's `auth_config` as the whole configuration and `{"type": "none"}` clearing it (rule 7), and the canonical token URL form of rule 15, at every write site; settings `connector.auth_enabled` and `trusted_oauth2_token_endpoints_regex` (the second read by no check before PR 2); audit-log redaction of `auth_config.client_secret`; removal of the inert `"auth": "Sig_V4"` from the Bedrock Claude 3 blueprint. Type `none` only; no I/O |
| Separate PR (#5228), before PR 2 | `ConnectorAddressValidator` extracted from `MLValidatableAsyncHttpClient` with today's rules unchanged; `validate` returns the validated addresses, and OkHttp streams connect only to them. No backport |
| Separate PR (#5233), before PR 2 | Rule 9 at execution for every connector with action URLs, at every execution site of the HTTP, AWS and Google executors, streaming included; the request builders take the checked URL and the header map; one substitution helper makes a parameter cycle a 400 at execution and at create, update and register. The backward-compatibility note above goes into its description and the release notes |
| PR 2 (#5234, draft) | `ml-algorithms`, with write-time checks in `common` and `plugin`: `client_credentials` with `client_secret_basic` / `client_secret_post` (`jwt-bearer` stays refused until PR 2b; other grants and `client_auth_method: none` until PR 3); the token client with its refused addresses and ports, layered on `ConnectorAddressValidator` and connecting only to the validated addresses; the process-wide cache (one request in flight per key, refresh-ahead, bounded backoff, the 10 s minimum token age of the 401 rule, a 60 s sweep of expired tokens) and the `oauth2_token_cache_max_seconds` setting; IdP error mapping; token sanitization and the bearer-header helper; `AuthorizationProviderFactory` (`oauth2` only), which re-runs the write-time checks; hooks in `HttpJsonConnectorExecutor` (predict and stream) with the https check on the URL rule 9 returns, the kill switch of rule 11 and the one-refresh budget in `ExecutionContext`; a 401 callback on the stream handler; cache wiring in `MachineLearningPlugin` and at the executor construction sites; the four node stats; the active-block write checks (the grant and client authentication methods PR 2 releases, `client_id` and `client_secret`, the write-time allowlist match, rules 2 and 3); the Azure OpenAI (Entra) blueprint and one generic OpenAI-compatible example; unit tests with an injected transport and a REST IT for the write paths and the refusals, with no address-policy override in any build. Ships in the same release as PR 1 |
| PR 2b | Google on the shared engine: `JwtAssertionSigner` (RS256), the `jwt-bearer` grant and the user-facing `jwt` block (`subject` optional); `GoogleConnectorExecutor` → subclass of `HttpJsonConnectorExecutor`, removing `authorizationValue` and the header override; `GoogleCredentialProvider` → ADC-only provider (`google_adc`); `auth_config` on `google_cloud`, with the synthesis from stored fields; the `jwt.*` protected fields of rule 8; Vertex AI blueprints gain a generic-form variant, legacy form kept; existing Google tests kept green (no `sub` in assertions); the `gemini/v1beta/generatecontent` streaming interface on `http` |
| PR 3 | Grants other than `client_credentials` and `jwt-bearer` (IBM IAM's vendor grant) and `client_auth_method: none` with `client_credentials`; `private_key_jwt`, `PS256`/`ES256`, optional `jwt.header` (`kid`, `x5t`); `${credential.*}` references inside `token_request_params`; blueprints for IBM watsonx, Databricks, SAP AI Core, Salesforce and Auth0/Okta/Keycloak gateways, which set the flag and append to the allowlist in one read-then-append `_cluster/settings` call (#5103 found 35 blueprints telling users to replace the list); documentation-website PR on validation timing and the flag |
| Done | Address validation for every OkHttp stream (#5206): the non-streaming rules before each stream, a direct connection and no redirects; streams to private destinations need `connector.private_ip_enabled`, and the private allowlist and restricted patterns apply |
| PR 4 (optional) | MCP executors on the same hook, after #4590 settles |

Size reference: #4921 was 46 files and +2,788 lines, about 1,300 of them tests. PR 1 is expected at about 1,500 added lines of main code and 6,000 of tests after the field rework (76 files, about 2,200 and 9,100 before it), and touches `build.gradle` only in test scope (a `testImplementation` dependency on `software.amazon.awssdk:dynamodb`). PR 2 is expected to need no `build.gradle` change outside test scope.

## Resolution of the review questions

The questions below were put to the community in revision 2 and answered in the #5171 thread (review of 2026-11-01 by the author of `google_cloud`, reply of 2026-11-03, follow-up and sign-off the same day). Two refinements were adopted: a declaration must carry a `type` naming a supported method, and `type` joined the protected fields of rule 8.

1. Configuration carrier: an `auth_config` object carried as the `parameters.auth` string, or a full top-level `auth` object with a version-gated stream field? *(Resolved 2026-11-03: `auth_config`, carried as the `parameters.auth` string. Reversed in revision 3.6, 2026-11-13: `auth_config` is a field of the connector in memory and on the transport, written and read only between nodes that run the feature's first release or later, and `auth` is no longer a reserved parameter key. Reasons: the field follows the pattern the connector's existing fields use, and the mixed-cluster concern that motivated the string form is answered by fixing the gate's version constant to the first release that ships the feature and by rule 5, which refuses writes that carry `auth_config` until every node runs it. The API, the storage form and the update semantics are unchanged; see Alternatives.)*
2. A separate token-endpoint allowlist with public-IdP defaults, or reuse of `trusted_connector_endpoints_regex`? *(Resolved: separate, with rules 8 and 15.)*
3. Default client authentication method? *(Resolved: no default; the field is required, rule 12.)*
4. `jwt-bearer` (RS256) in PR 2b for Google service accounts, `private_key_jwt` and the other algorithms in PR 3? *(Resolved: ordering kept.)*
5. Custom token-request headers? *(Resolved: out of v1.)*
6. `google_cloud` as a compatibility front door on the generic engine, deprecation deferred; the ADC provider as a soft dependency? *(Resolved: front door accepted by the connector's author, who will review PR 2b; the soft dependency is deferred to the deprecation discussion.)*
7. Pinned resolution on the OkHttp streaming path? *(Resolved: #5206 validates every stream before it opens; #5228, before PR 2, connects streams only to the validated addresses.)*

## References

- RFC 6749 §2.3.1, §4.4, §4.5; RFC 7523 §2.1–2.2; RFC 6750; RFC 8707; RFC 9700 §2.4.
- OpenSearch: #4231, #3208, #4915, #4921, #5041, #5058, #5071, #5079, #5097, #5103, #5131, #5135, #4590, #4571, #4971, #5003, #5166; community review of this RFC in the #5171 thread (2026-11-01 – 2026-11-03).
- Comparable designs: Kong `upstream-oauth` (`auth_method` ∈ client_secret_basic/post/private_key_jwt, `token_post_args`, `cache.default_ttl` 3600, purge on 401), AWS EventBridge API destination connections (refresh on 401/407 and within 60 s of expiry), Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity (`clientAuthenticationMethod` CLIENT_SECRET_BASIC | CLIENT_SECRET_POST | PRIVATE_KEY_JWT), Snowflake API_AUTHENTICATION integration (`OAUTH_CLIENT_AUTH_METHOD`, `OAUTH_GRANT`), Elasticsearch inference `azureopenai` (`client_id`/`client_secret`/`tenant_id`/`scopes`).
- Microsoft: disable local authentication for Azure AI services; Entra v2 client credentials flow. Google: service-account JWT-bearer token exchange (`https://oauth2.googleapis.com/token`).

milestone.title: M4 - Integrations
milestone.description: FTP + in-camera FTP; race-timing + print lab; outbound webhooks.

items.body:
## Summary
Establish the bounded `integrations` module that all third-party connectors plug into. Define a shared `integration_configs` table for storing per-tenant credentials, base URLs, feature flags, and connector state. All connectors (RunSignup, ChronoTrack, MyLaps, Bay Photo, SFTP, Drive, Dropbox) read configuration from this table.

## Acceptance criteria
- Given a tenant enables a connector in the admin UI,
  When credentials are saved,
  Then they are encrypted at rest (AES-256-GCM using a KMS-managed key) and never returned in plaintext via the API.
- Given a connector worker starts,
  When it loads its config,
  Then it reads from `integration_configs` and caches the decrypted credentials in memory only for the job lifetime.
- Given a connector is disabled,
  When the worker polls,
  Then no outbound calls are made and queued jobs are dropped with a logged reason.

## API surface
- `GET /api/integrations` — list available connector types and per-tenant status.
- `PUT /api/integrations/:type` — upsert credentials (admin-only, validates by attempting a test call).
- `DELETE /api/integrations/:type` — soft-delete, revokes credentials and stops workers.
- `POST /api/integrations/:type/test` — synchronous connectivity check.

## Schema changes
- `integration_configs(id, tenant_id, type, enabled, encrypted_credentials, config_json, last_synced_at, last_error, created_at, updated_at)`.
- Unique index on `(tenant_id, type)`.

## Feature-specific quality gates
- Credentials encrypted with envelope encryption; DEK rotation documented in runbook.
- No credentials ever logged, even at debug level (redaction middleware enforced in tests).
- Connector type is an enum; adding a new connector requires a migration.

## Test plan
- Unit tests for encryption round-trip and redaction.
- Integration test: enable, test, disable a stub connector via API.
- Verify decrypted creds never appear in API responses (snapshot test).

## Out of scope
- Specific connector implementations (separate issues).
- UI for admin config (covered by frontend epic).

### Universal quality gates (every PR)
- [ ] Tests: unit + integration; >=80% coverage on changed lines
- [ ] Lint + format clean
- [ ] Type safety: `tsc --noEmit` / `pyright` clean
- [ ] OpenAPI spec updated + validated; client SDK regenerated
- [ ] Migrations: forward + rollback tested
- [ ] Security: secret scan + dep audit clean
- [ ] Observability: traces + metrics emitted; logs structured
- [ ] Compliance: audit log entry if PII/biometric touched
- [ ] Docs updated (README / ADR / runbook)
- [ ] Performance budget honored (see roadmap.md)

items.title: create_conversation leaves its connector client open when the Bot Connector refuses the new conversation
items.body:
### What happens

`ChannelServiceAdapter.create_conversation` creates the connector client, then calls `conversations.create_conversation`, and registers `connector_client.close` on its `AsyncExitStack` only after that call has returned:

https://github.com/microsoft/Agents-for-python/blob/4e8d7f7ead9dfc7ae0c3ea83e22d59d553da8f1a/libraries/microsoft-agents-hosting-core/microsoft_agents/hosting/core/channel_service_adapter.py#L267-L317

When the create call raises, for example because the Bot Connector answers 403 or 429 or the request times out, the exit stack is never entered and the connector client is never closed. With 1.8.0 this leaves its aiohttp `ClientSession`, and the pooled connection, open: one per failed call, until garbage collection, which then logs `Unclosed client session` and `Unclosed connector`. An agent that retries a refused new conversation leaks one session per attempt.

The connector client also stays open if `create_user_token_client` raises, a few lines later. `process_proactive` has the same pattern the other way round: the user token client it creates first is not closed if `create_connector_client` raises.

### To reproduce

The script runs offline: a local server stands in for the Bot Connector and answers every `POST /v3/conversations` with the status given on the command line, and a fixed token stands in for the agent's token.

```python
"""ChannelServiceAdapter.create_conversation leaves its connector client open when the create call fails.

Runs offline: a local HTTP server stands in for the Bot Connector, and a fixed token stands in for the agent's token.
"""
import asyncio
import sys

import aiohttp
from aiohttp import web
from microsoft_agents.activity import Activity, ChannelAccount, ConversationParameters
from microsoft_agents.hosting.core.authorization import AnonymousTokenProvider, ConnectionManager
from microsoft_agents.hosting.fastapi import CloudAdapter

APP_ID = '00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000001'
TENANT_ID = '00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000002'


class FixedToken(AnonymousTokenProvider):
    async def get_access_token(self, resource_url: str, scopes: list[str], force_refresh: bool = False) -> str:
        return 'test-token'


SESSIONS: list[aiohttp.ClientSession] = []
_init = aiohttp.ClientSession.__init__


def _tracked_init(self: aiohttp.ClientSession, *args: object, **kwargs: object) -> None:
    _init(self, *args, **kwargs)
    SESSIONS.append(self)


aiohttp.ClientSession.__init__ = _tracked_init  # keep each session, to see whether it was closed


def open_sessions() -> int:
    return sum(not session.closed for session in SESSIONS)


async def main(status: int) -> None:
    async def connector(request: web.Request) -> web.Response:
        if status == 201:
            return web.json_response({'id': '19:channel@thread.tacv2;messageid=1', 'activityId': '1'}, status=201)
        return web.json_response({'error': {'code': 'Forbidden', 'message': 'refused'}}, status=status)

    app = web.Application()
    app.router.add_post('/v3/conversations', connector)
    runner = web.AppRunner(app)
    await runner.setup()
    site = web.TCPSite(runner, '127.0.0.1', 0)
    await site.start()
    service_url = f'http://127.0.0.1:{runner.addresses[0][1]}/'

    connections = ConnectionManager(provider_factory=lambda _: FixedToken(), CONNECTIONS={
        'SERVICE_CONNECTION': {'SETTINGS': {'CLIENTID': APP_ID, 'CLIENTSECRET': 'unused', 'TENANTID': TENANT_ID}}})
    adapter = CloudAdapter(connection_manager=connections)
    parameters = ConversationParameters(is_group=True, bot=ChannelAccount(id=f'28:{APP_ID}'), tenant_id=TENANT_ID,
                                        channel_data={'channel': {'id': '19:channel@thread.tacv2'}},
                                        activity=Activity(type='message', text='hello'))

    async def callback(context: object) -> None:
        pass

    for _ in range(3):
        try:
            await adapter.create_conversation(APP_ID, 'msteams', service_url, 'https://api.botframework.com', parameters,
                                              callback)
        except Exception as error:
            print(f'create_conversation raised {type(error).__name__}: {error}'.splitlines()[0])
    print(f'Bot Connector answered {status} to 3 calls; sessions opened: {len(SESSIONS)}, left open: {open_sessions()}')
    await runner.cleanup()


if __name__ == '__main__':
    asyncio.run(main(int(sys.argv[1]) if len(sys.argv) > 1 else 403))
```

```
$ python repro.py 403
create_conversation raised ClientResponseError: 403, message='Forbidden', url='http://127.0.0.1:42621/v3/conversations'
create_conversation raised ClientResponseError: 403, message='Forbidden', url='http://127.0.0.1:42621/v3/conversations'
create_conversation raised ClientResponseError: 403, message='Forbidden', url='http://127.0.0.1:42621/v3/conversations'
Bot Connector answered 403 to 3 calls; sessions opened: 3, left open: 3
$ python repro.py 201
Bot Connector answered 201 to 3 calls; sessions opened: 6, left open: 0
```

Seen with microsoft-agents-hosting-core 1.8.0 and microsoft-agents-hosting-fastapi 1.8.0, aiohttp 3.14.3, Python 3.12.16. `main` at 4e8d7f7ead9dfc7ae0c3ea83e22d59d553da8f1a creates and closes the clients in the same order.

### Expected

The connector client is closed whether or not the create call succeeds. Entering the `AsyncExitStack` before `create_connector_client`, and pushing each client's `close` as soon as the client exists, would do it, in `create_conversation` and in `process_proactive`.

**Story:** IDENTITY-P0-21 · **Phase:** F4 · **Plan:** `docs/WonderID/reference/WONDERID-FOUNDATION-DESIGN.md` §8.1 and §10 (integrator configurability, 2026-10-11)

**Goal.** Integrators set up user update rules and lifecycle rules from the catalogue in design §5.2.1, with simulation and report-only mode.

**Scope**
